entries.note: The proposition drops 'entire' and 'only.' The claim attributes an exclusive motive to the numbers' use.
This evaluates the usefulness of a metric and the quality of journalism.
'Mean very little' evaluates informational usefulness without specifying a factual threshold.
The proposition removes 'It appears' and turns rejection of an ethical explanation into a firm ethical verdict.
The central allegation concerns an intention to lift markets. The embedded revenue forecast is OpenAI's, not Zitron's.

entries.test: OpenAI's published guidance or public reporting of its internal projections would establish whether it projected roughly $30 billion in actual 2026 revenue.
entries.note: This concerns the existence of a projection, not whether the projected revenue materializes.

entries.test: Reported H1 2026 revenues for both companies and Anthropic's May run rate would establish the arithmetic difference.
entries.note: The figures given in the post total $27.9 billion, which is $20.1 billion below $48 billion, not $19.1 billion.
The opening assertion is endorsed despite the rhetorical question that follows. 'Marketing exercise' expresses his assessment of the reporting's value.
This is an insult. 'Rely on' narrows his criticism of simply 'using' the metric.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures and documented run-rate calculations would show how much underlying financial information is available and whether reported figures are inflated.
entries.note: The accountant remark is hyperbole, but the surrounding disclosure and inflation allegations have factual content.

entries.test: Company filings and public financial reporting available at publication would show which AI revenue figures were disclosed and whether Microsoft's sole available year was Bloomberg's FY2026 estimate.
entries.note: The proposition omits the specified fiscal year and the estimate's source and basis. 'We do not know' concerns public availability, not knowledge inside the companies.

entries.test: Microsoft's operational AI capacity records, public reporting, and quarterly capacity announcements would establish the approximately 2GW figure and the three claimed 1GW additions.
entries.note: Zitron adopts the approximately 2GW figure through his own reporting.

entries.test: A public disclosure of Cursor's actual operating revenues and costs after the SpaceX acquisition would falsify the prediction that they will never be publicly known.
entries.note: An indefinite 'never' forecast remains falsifiable by disclosure.
Actual annual revenue is checkable, but the claimed reason for withholding figures attributes a private motive.
'Likely less than $500 million' is explicitly probabilistic. Context identifies the revenue year as 2026.

entries.test: Customer concentration disclosures, customer identities, and subscription token allowances would establish whether the vast majority of the highest-spending 1% are AI startups offering token use above subscription revenue.
entries.note: The proposition weakens 'vast majority' to 'most' and removes 'from what I hear.' The source qualification does not itself turn the assertion into a probability claim.
The claim explains financial secrecy through an attributed motive. Token costs and resale prices alone cannot establish that motive.

entries.test: AI businesses' usage, incremental costs, losses, and customer-level margins would show whether increased demand causes larger losses and the most engaged customers are least profitable.
entries.note: This is a broad but testable assertion about unit economics.

entries.test: Harvey's revenue, operating costs, cash flows, and financing disclosures would show whether its product supports operations or the company depends entirely on venture funding.
entries.note: The surrounding text gives 'product-market fit' a concrete financial interpretation.

entries.test: Observed customer purchases and retention at prices covering service costs would test whether Harvey and other AI startups can obtain cost-covering demand.
entries.note: 'Will not pay' is stronger than 'do not actually want to pay.' The passage makes willingness to pay the cause of its product-market-fit conclusion.

entries.test: If AI startups lose continued fundraising access, subsequent customer spending and OpenAI and Anthropic revenue disclosures would show whether substantial revenue disappears.
entries.note: The antecedent is the loss of continuing startup funding; no deadline is supplied.

entries.test: Customer revenue concentration data and the relevant startups' revenue and token spending would establish the 80%, 1%, and 300%–1000% figures and customer composition.
entries.note: 'Mostly' weakens the source's 'vast majority.' The numerical claims remain directly checkable.

entries.test: AI startup financial statements, cash balances, and funding histories would show whether every startup loses money and consequently requires large capital raises every few months.
entries.note: The claim explicitly says losses necessitate the fundraising cadence.

entries.test: Revenue and startup token spending around each model release would show whether every release causes a large startup-funded revenue increase for Anthropic and OpenAI.
entries.note: The proposition omits the asserted magnitude, 'massive,' and the unrestricted token use.

entries.test: Customer revenue breakdowns and startup financing and spending records would show whether venture-funded startups sustain Anthropic's and OpenAI's revenues.
entries.note: The claim identifies an observable financing and customer-spending mechanism.

entries.test: Startup token procurement costs, subscription prices, and customer responses to cost-covering prices would test universal discounted resale and its claimed demand constraint.
entries.note: The proposition loses the explicit 'every AI startup' scope. 'Because' makes this a causal claim.
'Block' strengthens 'makes it harder.' The central claim attributes deliberate concealment and a private purpose.

entries.test: Available GPU contracts, realized rental prices, and data-center financial disclosures would establish whether actual prices and operating economics are publicly documented.
entries.note: Context makes this a claim about missing public financial information.

entries.test: SiliconData's index methodology, inputs, and weights would show the relative representation of spot prices and long-term contract rates.
entries.note: 'Mostly' weakens 'overwhelmingly.' Zitron endorses the spot-pricing allegation, not the imagined objection.

entries.test: The cited GPU rental contracts compared with contemporaneous quoted rates for the same hardware would establish whether multiple companies paid substantially less.
entries.note: The source reports repeated examples he found; the proposition broadens these into a general statement about companies' contracts.

entries.test: Canopy Wave's contract rates and the stated hardware cost and six-year depreciation assumptions would establish depreciation per GPU-hour and its share of revenue.
entries.note: The proposition omits the six-year depreciation horizon and its mismatch with the five-year contract.

entries.test: Operational capacity records and Microsoft's public commissioning claims would show whether available capacity is established and whether its announcements misrepresent capacity brought online.
entries.note: The public accuracy of Microsoft's capacity claims is testable without establishing its private motives.

entries.test: The sources and methodologies of published AI compute capacity estimates would show whether essentially all lack verified operational capacity data.
entries.note: Context gives 'guesses' the plain meaning of estimates unsupported by verified capacity records.

entries.test: Public commissioning records and supplier capacity disclosures would show whether at least 1GW of operational compute was available for Anthropic to acquire during the relevant period.
entries.note: 'I can find no compelling evidence' becomes the stronger 'there is no compelling evidence.' The 5GW forecast is attributed to investor statements reported by the New York Times.
'Most' weakens 'vast majority,' while the source says only several assumptions fall apart. There is no shared test for this aggregate characterization of fragile assumptions.
The overall verdict that known economics are 'extremely grim' is evaluative.

entries.test: Contract disclosures and financial statements would establish the total and uncancellable compute commitments and whether discounts or adjusted profits reduce or discharge those obligations.
entries.note: Zitron asserts the commitments and their persistence; the optimistic 2026 response belongs to the boosters he criticizes.

entries.test: Hyperscaler and AI lab customer revenue breakdowns, together with their customers' financing and cash flows, would establish revenue concentration and dependence on repeated funding.
entries.note: The proposition weakens both instances of 'vast majority' to 'most' and strengthens 'near-perpetual' to 'continual.'
This is an explicit evaluation and recommendation.

entries.test: Monthly lab revenues and startup token spending would test whether Anthropic or OpenAI can grow during periods when startup token spending does not increase.
entries.note: The proposition makes the indefinite horizon firm by dropping 'what appears to be.' The underlying monthly dependency claim is testable.
The claim caricatures coverage through absolute optimism. The proposition also drops the assertion about ignoring past bad events.
The source attributes an evasive purpose to every qualifying model. The proposition replaces that motive claim with a claim about what models omit.
This is an insult-laden warning without a shared factual test. The source says to distinguish types of promoters, not merely identify who is promoting the numbers.
